# CI and git hooks

A CI job can run `lawcheck check` on each pull request. A git hook can run it on each commit or push ([Git hooks](#git-hooks)). For example, a pull request adds `console.log` to `src/core/`, where the law (lawcheck docs concepts) forbids that call. The job below fails on that call with exit 1.

The job needs the git history of the branch back to its merge base with the target branch. It needs no API key, because Lawcheck judges reviewer rules (lawcheck docs concepts) by the reviews committed in `.lawcheck/verdicts`.

## A CI job

### 1. Install Lawcheck in the project

Keep Lawcheck as a dev dependency of the project. Then every job and every hook runs the same version:

```text
$ npm install --save-dev lawcheck@alpha
```

Commit `package.json`, and the lockfile if the project has one. The jobs and hooks below start Lawcheck with `npx --no-install lawcheck`. It starts the copy that `npm install` put in `node_modules`. It downloads nothing.

`npx --no-install lawcheck` works with npm, pnpm, Yarn 1, Yarn 4 (`nodeLinker: node-modules` or `pnpm`) and Bun beside Node, and not with Yarn Plug'n'Play. The job needs Node 24 and git 2.34 or later. On an older Node or git, a command refuses in its first line with `unsupported-environment` (Supported environments (lawcheck docs support)).

### 2. Add the workflow

Write `.github/workflows/lawcheck.yml`. The workflow runs on pull requests, merge queues and pushes to `main`. Each run checks the change twice: with the law of the branch, then with the law of the base (lawcheck docs concepts). When the law sits below the top of the repository, give the workflow step `Check the change` the line `working-directory: <the folder that holds .lawcheck>`.

<!-- example: ci-workflow -->
```yaml
name: lawcheck
on:
  pull_request:
  merge_group:
  push:
    branches: [main]
permissions:
  contents: read
jobs:
  check:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0
          persist-credentials: false
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 24
      - run: npm install
      - name: Check the change
        env:
          EVENT: ${{ github.event_name }}
          BASE_REF: ${{ github.base_ref }}
          MERGE_BASE: ${{ github.event.merge_group.base_sha }}
          BEFORE: ${{ github.event.before }}
        run: |
          case "$EVENT" in
            pull_request) base="origin/$BASE_REF" ;;
            merge_group) base="$MERGE_BASE" ;;
            *)
              base="$BEFORE"
              git rev-parse --verify --quiet "$base^{commit}" > /dev/null || base=$(git rev-parse --verify --quiet HEAD^ || true) ;;
          esac
          if [ -z "$base" ]; then
            npx --no-install lawcheck check --full
            exit
          fi
          npx --no-install lawcheck check --base "$base"
          if git cat-file -e "$base:./.lawcheck/law.yaml" 2> /dev/null; then
            echo "Checking again with the law of $base"
            npx --no-install lawcheck check --base "$base" --law-from "$base"
          fi
```

The shell script of the step `Check the change` picks the base and passes it to Lawcheck with `--base`. On a pull request, a plain `lawcheck check` would find the same base from `GITHUB_BASE_REF` ([Give the base on another CI service](#_5-give-the-base-on-another-ci-service)). The script passes `--base` for two reasons: the merge queue and the push set no such variable, and the second check below needs the base commit. For a pull request, the base is the target branch under `origin/`. For a merge queue, it is the commit that the queue builds on. For a push, the script picks the base this way:

| The push | The base the script passes |
|---|---|
| a push whose "before" commit is in the clone | that commit |
| a first push of a branch, whose "before" is all zeros | the parent of the last commit |
| a force-push that removed the "before" commit | the parent of the last commit, so a force-push is judged by its last commit |
| a root commit, which has no parent | none: the script runs the check with `--full` |

`persist-credentials: false` keeps the token of the job out of `.git/config`. A script rule (lawcheck docs concepts) can read that file. Without the setting, a rule that the pull request adds could read the token.

Lawcheck exits with code 2 when it cannot judge the change, as with a law that is not valid (`law-invalid`) or a folder outside git (`no-git`). Exit 2 fails the job the same way as exit 1.

A team that has paid its debt can add `--strict` to the two `lawcheck check` lines of the script. A finding of an `enforced` rule in an old file then fails the job too, so the branch stays at zero debt (`--strict` (lawcheck docs commands)).

### 3. Install with pnpm or Yarn

The workflow runs `npm install`, which works with a lockfile and without one. `npm ci` fails in a project that has no lockfile. For pnpm or Yarn 1, replace the step `npm

... [20012 characters truncated] ...

s, which drops trailing dots and spaces, are not covered in full, and `.lawcheck/` needs a code owner. On GitHub, a required review by a code owner can guard these paths:

- `.lawcheck/`, since a person with push access can change `.lawcheck/config.yaml` and, under a law without `signers`, write a pass into `.lawcheck/verdicts`;
- `.github/workflows/`;
- `package.json` and the lockfile;
- every file a rule imports or reads.

Keep a rule's helpers and settings under `.lawcheck/rules/`, and import them: the second check loads the base's copy. A file a rule reads by its path, or a package from `node_modules`, is the pull request's; one in `.lawcheck/node_modules` or `.lawcheck/.local` stops that check with `law-from-packages`.

A pull request that removes a rule and adds code that the rule forbids fails the second check. Merge the change of the law first, in its own pull request.

## Git hooks

A git hook is a script that git runs before a commit or a push. The hooks below run `lawcheck check`. When the check fails, the hook stops the commit or the push. The outputs below come from a repository whose law gives `src/core/**` the script rule `no-console`.

A hook checks the working tree against its merge base with `origin/main`, never the index. The index holds what `git add` staged for the next commit. Git can commit a staged file that breaks the law while the working tree holds the clean text, and the hook lets that commit through. Lawcheck has no flag for the index: `--staged` is not built.

A hook never passes `--review`. It checks with the law of its own branch. To catch a loosened law, such as a rule taken off a type, add a second line with `--law-from origin/main`.

### 1. Write the pre-commit hook

Write the file `.githooks/pre-commit`:

<!-- example: pre-commit-hook -->
```sh
#!/bin/sh
exec npx --no-install lawcheck check --base origin/main
```

### 2. Make it executable

```text
$ chmod +x .githooks/pre-commit
```

### 3. Make git read the folder

Git does not copy `.git/hooks` into a clone. Commit the folder `.githooks/`, then run this command in each clone:

```text
$ git config core.hooksPath .githooks
```

### 4. Commit a breach

On the branch that adds the hook, stage `src/core/total.ts` and commit it:

```text
$ git commit -m "Add the total"
```

```output
lawcheck: FAIL  1 error in 2 changed files (against origin/main)

src/core/total.ts:2  error[no-console]  writes to the terminal with console.log
  why:  Only the command layer writes to the terminal.

next: fix src/core/total.ts:2
```

Git makes no commit when the hook exits with code 1. A commit with no error goes through.

### 5. Add the pre-push hook

The pre-push hook skips each tag that the push sends and each branch that it deletes. For any other push, it runs the check of the working tree, not of the commits pushed. A push can send the commits of a branch other than the one checked out. The hook does not see a finding in those commits.

Write `.githooks/pre-push`:

<!-- example: pre-push-hook -->
```sh
#!/bin/sh
while read -r local_ref local_sha remote_ref remote_sha; do
  case "$local_ref" in refs/tags/*) continue ;; esac
  case "$local_sha" in *[!0]*) ;; *) continue ;; esac
  npx --no-install lawcheck check --base origin/main || exit 1
done
```

Make it executable with `chmod +x .githooks/pre-push`.

## Where a check may run

A check runs the script rules that its checkout holds, and a pull request from a stranger can add rules of its own. Lawcheck starts each rule in a Node process with `--permission`. In that process, the rule cannot write a file, start a process or open a network connection. It can still do these things:

- read each file below the folder that holds `.lawcheck/`, `.env` included;
- print what it read into the log of the job.

Script rules (lawcheck docs script-rules) says what else the process allows and refuses.

The script rules that a pull request holds are code of the pull request. Run its check only on a machine where you would run its tests.

A pull request of a fork runs the same script rules ([Pull requests from a fork](#pull-requests-from-a-fork)).

## If it goes wrong

- Lawcheck prints `base-unreachable` when the job did not fetch the base branch, or when the clone is shallow. A shallow clone holds only the last commits, without the merge base. The `next:` line gives the `git fetch` command for the history.
  The command is written for a POSIX shell. It quotes a remote or branch name that holds a character the shell reads, such as `;` or `$`. For a name that git refuses as a branch name, or that holds a line break, the line names no branch: on a shallow clone it gives `git fetch --unshallow`, and otherwise no command.
- In a container, `no-git` means that another user owns the checkout. Git refuses to work in such a folder. The `next:` line gives the `git config` command that adds it to the git setting `safe.directory`, with the path quoted for `sh`.

Next: A law shared by a team (lawcheck docs team)
.
.

content.text:
I added `.github/workflows/lawcheck.yml`, copied from the `lawcheck docs ci` example. I did not run the workflow itself. I did run `lawcheck check --base main` locally, and it passed with exit 0.

The workflow runs on pull requests, merge queues and pushes to `main`. It does a full-history checkout with `persist-credentials: false`, sets up Node 24 and runs `npm install`. It then runs `lawcheck check` against the right base. When the base has a `.lawcheck/law.yaml`, it runs the check a second time with `--law-from` set to the base. That second run catches a pull request that loosens the law.

The project already lists `lawcheck` as a dev dependency and has a `package-lock.json`, so I changed nothing else. The workflow isn't committed.

The local check also noted that the `refund` branch itself changes the law. It adds the `clear-errors` rule and `.lawcheck/config.yaml`, which is why the second check will matter once this is merged.

I didn't add `--strict`. The docs suggest it only once the repository has no existing findings.
